authored.title: Jaeng (the four moat corners)
authored.body_html:
What this is

แจ่ง (chaeng) is the Lanna word for corner — standard Thai says มุม (mum) — and in Chiang Mai the word survives chiefly in four proper names: the four bastions where the old city's moat turns its right angles. Going clockwise from the northeast: แจ่งศรีภูมิ (Chaeng Si Phum, in the older pronunciation สะหลีภูมิ sali phum — ศรี glory, Skt. śrī + ภูมิ ground, Skt. bhūmi), แจ่งก๊ะต๊ำ (Chaeng Katam — a katam is a bamboo fish trap), แจ่งกู่เฮือง (Chaeng Ku Hueang — กู่ ku, a reliquary stupa + เฮือง hueang, of which more below), and แจ่งหัวลิน (Chaeng Hua Lin — หัว head + ลิน lin, a water conduit in the northern tongue). The names are a map of their own: water enters the moat at the head-of-the-conduit corner, the highest ground, and leaves past the fish trap at the lowest.

They are not ruins with plaques. Every June the city's annual blessing (ทำบุญเมือง — สืบชะตาเมือง, the suep chata rite performed for a whole city) is held simultaneously at ten stations: the five gates, the four แจ่ง, and the navel. The corners still work.

The four, by name

ศรีภูมิ — northeast. The auspicious ground. Tradition — the chronicle tradition begins the city's construction at this corner, and the taksa scheme (below) places ศรี, glory, in its sector. When the mediumship rites were separated from the court-run Inthakhin festival around 1900, it was to Chaeng Si Phum that the medium elements were relegated (Tanabe 2000:308) — the corner as the keeping-place for what the center set down.

ก๊ะต๊ำ — southeast. The lowest corner, where the moat's water finds its way out; the fish trap is the etymology the sources agree on, and it is a working image — where water leaves, fish gather, and a trap goes. A shrine stands at this corner today: the ศาลเจ้าพ่อหลักเมืองแจ่งกระต๊ำ, a city-pillar-lord shrine keeping the corner in the present tense. (Note the shrine's own sign spells it กระต๊ำ against the more common ก๊ะต๊ำ — the word is Lanna and the spellings float.)

กู่เฮือง — southwest. The corner in the กาลกิณี (kalakini, misfortune) sector of the taksa wheel, in the quarter through which the dead traditionally leave the city. The name-story in circulation — that the กู่ holds or honours a jailer, หมื่นเฮือง (Mün Hueang, หมื่น being the rank) — is graded REPORTED in this wiki's citation basis: one secondary source, no primary attestation found yet. Inference — a plainer reading also exists: เฮือง is the northern cognate of เรือง, glowing, which would make the name simply "the shining reliquary." Which reading the leaf supports is an open question below.

หัวลิน — northwest. The head of the ลิน, the conduit that fed the moat from the Huay Kaeo stream off Doi Suthep — documented water engineering, not just a name (Fine Arts Department, Office 7). The northwest is the high corner; the whole square drinks from here. Wat Lok Molee stands on the outer bank a short walk east along the north wall.

The wheel behind the corners

Tradition, documented — the ทักษาเมือง (taksa mueang) scheme reads the city as born on a Thursday and lays the eight taksa qualities clockwise from west: บริวาร retinue (W) → อายุ longevity (NW) → เดช power (N) → ศรี glory (NE) → มูละ wealth (E) → อุตสาหะ industry (SE) → มนตรี counsel (S) → กาลกิณี misfortune (SW), with เกตุ at the navel. The scheme is solidly documented as tradition — and the scholarship holds it was formalized after the founding era (Tilokarat and later), so it explains how the city has been read for centuries, not necessarily what its founder intended in 1296. The corners inherit their characters from this wheel: ศรีภูมิ the glory corner, กู่เฮือง the kalakini one — which is also why the customary lap of the moat keeps the southwest quarter for transit rather than destination.

What the shelf says

Checked against this catalogue on 2026-08-27: no manuscript title in the collection names a corner — not แจ่ง, not any of the four names, in any script or romanisation the titles use. Zero is the finding, and it says something true: the แจ่ง tradition is kept in brick, in rite, and in speech — an architecture-and-observance tradition rather than a palm-leaf one. The places where the corners should surface in writing are the city chronicles (tamnan) and the founding narratives — see the open questions. The entity's aliases stand ready; the day a crawl brings in a tamnan witness that names a แจ่ง, the counter above this article will say so.

Still alive

  • The June city-blessing at ten points — five gates, four แจ่ง, the navel, fireworks-coordinated — runs annually under the municipality (documented in official announcements, 2025 and 2026).
  • The corpse-gate custom persists: the dead do not leave by Chiang Mai Gate but by แสนปุง in the southwest, and residents observe it.
  • Municipal lamp-offerings at the four แจ่ง during Yi Peng are reported in official material — a photograph with a date would firm this to solid.
  • Street directions in the city still say แจ่ง unselfconsciously — hearing the word means the old city is near. The street-level companion to this article, with nine ways to tell inside from outside, lives at motdang.net/moat.html.

Open questions

1. The Mün Hueang story. REPORTED only. To settle: ตำนานพื้นเมืองเชียงใหม่ (Wyatt & Aroonrut's translation is already in this wiki's citation base for the founding ritual, p. 78 — does the corner story appear?); Sanguan Chotisukharat's ประชุมตำนานลานนาไทย (1971); Sarassawadee Ongsakul's History of Lan Na; and the Fine Arts Department Office 7 restoration records for the southwest bastion — the sharpest question being whether an actual กู่ structure is attested at the corner at all. 2. แจ่ง on the leaf. Do any tamnan witnesses in the wider corpora (DREAMSEA, EAP scans of the Chiang Mai chronicle recensions) name the corners? A single attestation would date the names. 3. The Yi Peng lamp rite at the corners — wants one dated official citation or a dated photograph. 4. Retellings to treat cautiously (from the citation basis): "Suan Prung = disembowelling," "Katam is unlucky," corpses-via-Suan-Dok, and reading the taksa wheel as the founder's 1296 intent. This article repeats none of them.

Sources

The graded citation spine for everything above is `mueang-map/data/canonical/auspicious-basis.md` (SOLID / REPORTED / UNVERIFIED per claim, with links). Principal anchors: Chiang Mai Municipality's gate-and-corner page and city-blessing announcements [official]; Fine Arts Department Office 7 on the Mae Kha–moat water system [official]; Wyatt & Aroonrut (trans.), The Chiang Mai Chronicle, 1998, p. 78; Tanabe, "Autochthony and the Inthakhin Cult of Chiang Mai," in Turton (ed.), Civility and Savagery, 2000, 294–318; Swearer, Premchit & Dokbuakaew, Sacred Mountains of Northern Thailand, 2004; Denes & Pradit, JUCR 25 (2022); Sanguan Chotisukharat, ประชุมตำนานลานนาไทย, 1971.
